specStatements.text: When a force causes an object to move through a distance work is done on the object. So a force does work on an object when the force causes a displacement of the object.
The work done by a force on an object can be calculated using the equation:
work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force)
work done, W, in joules, J
One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.
Students should be able to describe the energy transfer involved when work is done.
Students should be able to convert between newton-metres and joules.
Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object.

concepts.definition: When a force causes an object to move through a distance, work is done on the object. A force does work on an object when the force causes a displacement of the object; a force that causes no displacement does no work, however large it is or however long it is applied.

The movement of the object caused by the force. Work is done only when the force produces a displacement, so both a force and a movement are needed. If the object does not move, there is no displacement and no work is done by that force.

concepts.term: Distance moved along the line of action of the force
concepts.definition: The distance used in the work done equation is the distance the object moves along the line of action of the force, that is, the distance moved in the direction in which the force acts. Movement at right angles to a force is not distance along its line of action, so that force does no work.

The work done by a force on an object can be calculated using: work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force), written in symbols as W = F s. This equation is not given on the exam equation sheet, so it must be recalled and applied.

concepts.term: Symbols and units in W = F s
concepts.definition: In W = F s: work done, W, in joules, J; force, F, in newtons, N; distance, s, in metres, m. The distance must be in metres before it is substituted, so a distance given in centimetres or kilometres has to be converted first.

The joule, J, is the unit of work done. One joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre. So a 1 N force moving an object 2 m along its line of action does 2 J of work.

Multiplying newtons by metres gives newton-metres, and 1 joule = 1 newton-metre. The two units are identical in size, so converting between them changes only the name and never the number: 350 N m of work is 350 J of work.

Doing work is one way of transferring energy. The work done by a force on an object, in joules, is the energy transferred by that force, in joules. Work done and energy transferred are therefore the same quantity measured in the same unit.

concepts.term: Describing the energy transfer when work is done
concepts.definition: Describe the transfer by naming the store energy comes from and the store it goes to. Lifting a box steadily: chemical store of the person to the gravitational potential store of the box. Pushing a trolley to speed it up: chemical store of the person to the kinetic store of the trolley. Braking a car: kinetic store of the car to thermal store of the brakes.

Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object. Dragging a crate across a rough floor, or braking a bicycle, transfers energy to thermal stores, so the surfaces that rub together become warmer.

misconceptions.question: A shopper stands still holding a heavy bag at their side for two minutes. Is work done on the bag?
misconceptions.correct: No work is done on the bag by the upward force, because the force causes no displacement of the bag.
misconceptions.misconception: I am pushing or holding really hard and it feels like effort, so I must be doing work on it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English 'work' means effort, and holding a heavy object is tiring, so students judge work by how hard it feels rather than by whether the object moves.
misconceptions.correction: In physics, work is done only when a force causes a displacement. With no movement, s = 0, so W = F × 0 = 0 J of work is done on the bag no matter how tiring holding it is.

misconceptions.question: A machine does 4500 N m of work. What is this in joules?
misconceptions.correct: 4500 J, because 1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so the number does not change.
misconceptions.misconception: Newton-metres and joules are different sizes, so I have to multiply or divide by 1000 to swap between them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every other conversion students meet (mm to m, g to kg, kJ to J) involves a factor of 10, 100 or 1000, so they expect a factor here too.
misconceptions.correction: The newton-metre and the joule are the same unit under two names: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre. Converting changes the words only, so 4500 N m = 4500 J.

misconceptions.question: A porter carries a suitcase 20 m along a level corridor. How much work does the upward supporting force do on the suitcase?
misconceptions.correct: None. The suitcase moves horizontally, so it moves no distance along the line of action of the upward force.
misconceptions.misconception: The suitcase moved 20 m and there was a force on it, so I multiply the force by 20 m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn W = F s as 'force times distance' and substitute whatever distance the question gives, without checking the direction that distance was travelled in.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is work done = force × distance moved along the line of action of the force. Horizontal movement is at right angles to the upward force, so that distance is zero and the upward force does no work.

misconceptions.question: A crate is dragged across a rough floor. What happens to the energy transferred by the pushing force?
misconceptions.correct: It is transferred to thermal stores; the temperature of the crate and the floor rises.
misconceptions.misconception: Friction uses the energy up, so that energy is lost and no longer exists.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Teachers and textbooks say energy is 'lost to friction', and the warming is too small to feel, so students conclude the energy has gone rather than moved.
misconceptions.correction: Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object. The energy is transferred to thermal stores, not destroyed.

misconceptions.question: A box is lifted steadily from the floor onto a shelf. Which store of the box gains energy?
misconceptions.correct: The gravitational potential store, because the box is raised at a steady speed and does not get faster.
misconceptions.misconception: Work is being done on the box, so the box must be speeding up and gaining energy in its kinetic store.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The first example of work most students meet is a force accelerating an object, so they attach work permanently to movement getting faster.
misconceptions.correction: Work done transfers energy, but not always to the kinetic store. Lifting at a steady speed fills the gravitational potential store; dragging against friction fills thermal stores.

misconceptions.question: Two students each push a bench 3 m with a force of 40 N. One takes 5 s, the other takes 20 s. Who does more work?
misconceptions.correct: Neither. Both do 120 J of work, because work done = force × distance and both force and distance are the same.
misconceptions.misconception: The one who kept pushing for longer did more work, because work depends on how long you keep the force on.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language ties work to time spent, and time appears in the closely related idea of power, so students smuggle time into W = F s.
misconceptions.correction: Time does not appear in W = F s. Work done depends only on the force and the distance moved along its line of action; how quickly the work is done is power, a different quantity.

misconceptions.question: A force of 25 N moves an object 80 m along its line of action. What is the work done?
misconceptions.correct: 2000 J, from W = F s = 25 N × 80 m.
misconceptions.misconception: You divide to get work done, so it is 25 ÷ 80, or maybe 80 ÷ 25.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet several equations of the form quantity = quantity ÷ quantity (speed, density, pressure) and apply that pattern to W = F s without checking it.
misconceptions.correction: W = F s means work done = force multiplied by distance. Dividing gives neither joules nor a sensible size; multiply the force by the distance moved along its line of action.

misconceptions.question: Is the newton-metre a unit of force or a unit of work done?
misconceptions.correct: It is a unit of work done: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre.
misconceptions.misconception: It has 'newton' in the name, so a newton-metre must measure force, just a bigger force.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read compound units as belonging to the first unit named, and newtons are strongly linked to force from the start of the forces topic.
misconceptions.correction: A newton-metre comes from multiplying a force in newtons by a distance in metres, which is work done. It equals one joule; force is measured in newtons alone.

misconceptions.question: A cyclist brakes hard for a long time on a hill. What happens to the brake blocks?
misconceptions.correct: Their temperature rises, because work is done against the frictional forces acting on them.
misconceptions.misconception: Friction just slows things down; something has to be heated by a flame or a heater before its temperature can rise.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Temperature rise is first taught alongside heating, so students file friction under 'slowing down' and never connect it to a rise in temperature.
misconceptions.correction: Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object. Brake blocks, drills and rubbed hands all get hotter for this reason.

misconceptions.question: A force of 12 N pushes a book 50 cm along the line of action of the force. What is the work done?
misconceptions.correct: 6 J, because 50 cm is 0.50 m and W = 12 N × 0.50 m.
misconceptions.misconception: The numbers in the question are 12 and 50, so the work done is 12 × 50 = 600 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students substitute the numbers as printed and only check units at the end, if at all, so a distance in centimetres slips through unconverted.
misconceptions.correction: In W = F s the distance, s, is in metres. Convert first: 50 cm = 0.50 m, giving W = 12 × 0.50 = 6 J.

misconceptions.question: Which quantities are measured in joules?
misconceptions.correct: Work done and energy transferred are both measured in joules, and 1 joule = 1 newton-metre.
misconceptions.misconception: Joules are for heat and food energy; mechanical work must be measured in some other unit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Joules are usually met first in heating and in nutrition labels, so students tie the unit to those contexts rather than to energy transfer in general.
misconceptions.correction: Doing work is a way of transferring energy, so work done is measured in the same unit as energy: the joule. A newton-metre of work is a joule of energy transferred.

mcqs.stem: In which of these situations is work done on the object by the force described?

options.text: A sledge is pulled forwards and slides 4 m along the ground
options.rationale: The pulling force causes a displacement of the sledge along its own line of action, so work is done on the sledge.

options.text: A shopper stands still holding a heavy bag for a minute
options.rationale: It feels like hard work, but the bag does not move, so the upward force causes no displacement and does no work.

options.text: A waiter walks 5 m holding a loaded tray level in one hand
options.rationale: The tray moves, but horizontally, so it moves no distance along the line of action of the upward force.

options.text: A driver pushes a stalled van hard but it will not budge
options.rationale: A large force is applied for a long time, but with no displacement there is no work done on the van.

mcqs.stem: A student holds a box weighing 40 N at a constant height for 15 s. How much work does the student's upward force do on the box?

options.rationale: This is 40 × 15, using the time in seconds as if it were the distance in metres.
This is 40 ÷ 15, dividing instead of multiplying, and still using time as a distance.

options.text: 0 J
options.rationale: The box has no displacement, so s = 0 and W = 40 × 0 = 0 J.
This quotes the force as if a force in newtons were itself an amount of work in joules.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist pushes a broken bike with a steady force of 25 N along the line of action of the force, moving it 80 m. What is the work done on the bike?

options.rationale: This is 25 ÷ 80, treating W = F s as though work were force divided by distance.
This is 80 ÷ 25, the same division error carried out the other way round.
This adds the force and the distance instead of multiplying them.

mcqs.stem: Which symbol equation matches 'work done = force × distance (moved along the line of action of the force)'?

options.text: W = F / s
options.rationale: Students copy the pattern of speed = distance ÷ time and divide rather than multiply.

options.text: W = F s
options.rationale: Work done, W, is the force, F, multiplied by the distance, s, moved along its line of action.

options.text: F = W s
options.rationale: A rearrangement error: this makes force the product, which does not match the words given.

options.text: s = W F
options.rationale: Another mis-rearrangement, making distance the product of work done and force.

mcqs.stem: In the equation W = F s, which units belong with each quantity?

options.text: W in newtons, F in joules, s in metres
options.rationale: The newton is attached to the quantity whose name sounds bigger, swapping the units for W and F.

options.text: W in joules, F in newtons, s in metres
options.rationale: This is exactly the specification's list: work done in J, force in N, distance in m.

options.text: W in joules, F in newtons, s in centimetres
options.rationale: Distances are often measured in centimetres in class, so the metre requirement is overlooked.

options.text: W in watts, F in newtons, s in metres
options.rationale: Work is confused with power, which does depend on time and is measured in watts.

mcqs.stem: One joule of work is done in which of these situations?

options.text: A force of one newton acts on an object for one second
options.rationale: Time is substituted for distance, because work is wrongly thought to depend on how long a force acts.

options.text: A force of one newton moves an object 1 m sideways
options.rationale: Movement at right angles to the force is not distance along its line of action, so no work is done.

options.text: A force of one newton is applied but nothing moves
options.rationale: Applying a force is not enough; without a displacement the work done is zero.

options.text: A force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of one joule of work done.

mcqs.stem: A machine does 4500 N m of work. What is this work done in joules?

options.rationale: A factor of 1000 is applied, as if newton-metres were kilojoules.
1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so the number is unchanged and only the unit's name differs.
A factor of 100 is divided out, again assuming the two units are different sizes.
The value is divided by 1000, converting in the wrong direction by an invented factor.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about newton-metres and joules is correct?

options.text: 1 newton-metre of work is equal to 1000 joules of work
options.rationale: A factor of 1000 is assumed by analogy with kilojoules and other metric conversions.

options.text: The newton-metre measures force, the joule measures work
options.rationale: The unit is read as belonging to newtons, so it is filed under force rather than work done.

options.text: The newton-metre measures work, the joule measures heat
options.rationale: Joules are met first in heating, so the unit is tied to that context instead of to energy in general.

options.text: 1 newton-metre of work is exactly equal to 1 joule of work
options.rationale: The specification states 1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so the two units are identical in size.

mcqs.stem: A student lifts a box steadily from the floor onto a shelf. Which best describes the energy transfer as work is done on the box?

options.text: Chemical store of the student to the kinetic store of the box as it rises
options.rationale: Work is assumed always to speed an object up, but the box is lifted at a steady speed.

options.text: Gravitational potential store of the box to chemical store of the student
options.rationale: The direction of transfer is reversed; this would describe the box lowering and driving the student.

options.text: Chemical store of the student to gravitational potential store of the box
options.rationale: The lifting force causes an upward displacement, and the box ends up higher, so its gravitational potential store fills.

options.text: Chemical store of the student is used up and is not transferred anywhere
options.rationale: Energy is treated as being consumed by effort rather than transferred to another store.

mcqs.stem: A car brakes and comes to rest. Work is done against the frictional forces at the brakes. Which best describes what happens?

options.text: The kinetic store of the car empties and the energy is destroyed
options.rationale: 'Energy lost to friction' is read as energy ceasing to exist rather than being transferred.

options.text: The kinetic store of the car empties and the brakes rise in temperature
options.rationale: Work done against friction transfers energy to thermal stores, so the temperature of the brakes rises.

options.text: The kinetic store empties and the brakes stay at the same temperature
options.rationale: Friction is seen only as a slowing effect, disconnected from any rise in temperature.

options.text: The thermal store of the brakes empties into the car's kinetic store
options.rationale: The transfer is described backwards; this would speed the car up rather than stop it.

mcqs.stem: What is the effect of work being done against the frictional forces acting on an object?

options.text: The energy of the object is destroyed
options.rationale: Energy is thought to be used up by friction instead of transferred to thermal stores.

options.text: The object slows but does not warm
options.rationale: Friction is linked only to slowing down, never to a rise in temperature.

options.text: The temperature of the object falls
options.rationale: The phrase 'energy is lost' is taken to mean the object cools rather than warms.

options.text: The temperature of the object rises
options.rationale: This is exactly what the specification states happens when work is done against friction.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist brakes for a long time going downhill and the brake blocks become hot. Why?

options.text: Friction destroys the bike's energy and heat is what is left over
options.rationale: Energy is imagined to be destroyed, with heat treated as a by-product rather than the transfer itself.

options.text: The blocks gain energy in their kinetic store and so become hot
options.rationale: Work done is assumed to fill a kinetic store, even though the blocks are not moving faster.

options.text: The rider squeezes the levers hard, and squeezing hard makes heat
options.rationale: The size of the force alone is credited, with no attention to the distance moved against friction.

options.text: Work is done against friction, so the blocks rise in temperature
options.rationale: The blocks rub on the moving wheel, and work done against those frictional forces raises their temperature.

mcqs.stem: A porter carries a 60 N suitcase 20 m along a level corridor, keeping it at a constant height. How much work does the upward supporting force do on the suitcase?

options.rationale: This is 60 × 20, using the horizontal distance even though it is at right angles to the force.

options.text: 3 J
options.rationale: This is 60 ÷ 20, dividing the force by the distance instead of multiplying.

options.text: 0 J
options.rationale: The suitcase moves horizontally, so the distance moved along the line of action of the upward force is zero.
The force in newtons is quoted as if it were the work done in joules.

mcqs.stem: A box is dragged 5 m by a steady 30 N force. It is then dragged 10 m by the same 30 N force. How does the work done compare?

options.text: It stays the same, because the same size of force is used on both journeys
options.rationale: Work is judged by the force alone, as if the distance moved did not enter the equation.

options.text: It quadruples, because the force and the distance have both been doubled
options.rationale: The force is misread as doubling too, giving a factor of four instead of two.

options.text: It doubles, because work done is force × distance and the distance doubles
options.rationale: W = F s with F unchanged and s doubled from 5 m to 10 m, so 150 J becomes 300 J.

options.text: It halves, because the same force is now spread over a longer distance
options.rationale: Work is treated as force divided by distance, so a longer distance appears to reduce it.

mcqs.stem: A force of 12 N pushes a book 50 cm across a desk along the line of action of the force. What is the work done on the book?

options.text: 6 J

options.rationale: The distance is substituted as 50 without converting centimetres to metres.
This is 12 ÷ 50, dividing rather than multiplying and leaving the distance unconverted.
The force and the unconverted distance are added instead of multiplied.

mcqs.stem: A cleaner pushes a trolley at a steady speed across a rough floor with a force of 25 N for 8 m, doing 200 J of work. What happens to that 200 J?

options.text: It is transferred to thermal stores, so the trolley rises in temperature
options.rationale: The speed is steady, so the work is done against friction, and that raises the temperature of the object.

options.text: It is transferred to the kinetic store, so the trolley gets faster and faster
options.rationale: Work done is assumed always to speed an object up, but the trolley moves at a steady speed.

options.text: It is used up in overcoming friction, so that energy no longer exists
options.rationale: Friction is treated as destroying energy rather than transferring it to thermal stores.

options.text: It is transferred to the gravitational potential store of the trolley
options.rationale: The floor is level, so the trolley is not raised and that store does not fill.
